title: Prototype-based Correlation Transfer for Sketch-based Image Retrieval with Incomplete Modality Streams

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Continual Learning Sketch-based Image Retrieval with Missing Data (CIM-SBIR) and proposes Prototype-based Correlation Transfer (PCT) to handle emerging classes and incomplete modalities, achieving strong performance while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Existing SBIR methods assume fixed data sizes and complete paired sketch-image modalities, which fails in real-world scenarios where classes grow continuously and some modalities are missing.
AI.method: The proposed PCT approach uses an adapter to fine-tune pre-trained models for continual learning, a graph attention-based scheme to capture inter-modal correlations for prototype-guided modality completion, and a consensual semantic constraint to preserve representation consistency across incremental sessions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across several datasets show that PCT performs effectively even when modalities are missing while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Prototype-based Correlation Transfer provides an effective solution for continual sketch-based image retrieval under incomplete modality streams.

title: Shorter Chains via Macro Transitions: Constant-Factor Compression for Chain-of-Thought Counter Simulation

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two machine rewrites, order-k macro transitions and base-b counting, to compress chain-of-thought counter machine simulations by a constant factor while preserving exact language recognition and length generalization under moderate compression.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought constructions that make transformers Turing complete typically simulate one counter machine transition per token, making serial generation length proportional to runtime and creating a major computational cost.
AI.method: The authors propose order-k macro transitions that combine k reachable base transitions into one token (compressing length T to roughly T/k with vocabulary bounded by the base vocabulary raised to k) and base-b counting that processes b counter units per token during monotone decrement bursts, keeping both within the same CoT counter programming class.
AI.result: On six synthetic counter machine tasks including equal-count and three-sum arithmetic verification, transformers trained on compressed traces achieve the predicted trace-length reductions along with lower generation latency, fewer attention operations, and smaller key-value caches, while retaining length generalization under moderate compression and degrading in accuracy when compression becomes aggressive relative to the counting range.
AI.conclusion: Constant-factor compression via macro transitions and base-b counting reduces serial CoT generation cost without sacrificing exact recognition or length generalization within moderate compression regimes, though aggressive compression trades off accuracy and increases reachable vocabulary data scaling cost.

title: A Survey of Advancing Audio Super-Resolution and Bandwidth Extension from Discriminative to Generative Models

AI.tldr: This survey reviews audio super-resolution and bandwidth extension, tracing the shift from discriminative deterministic mapping models to generative modeling approaches and providing controlled empirical comparisons across representative methods.
AI.motivation: Audio super-resolution and bandwidth extension are inherently ill-posed because high-frequency content is missing, and early discriminative deep neural networks suffer from regression-to-the-mean effects and spectral over-smoothing.
AI.method: The survey categorizes and examines discriminative DNNs alongside generative approaches including autoregressive models, VAEs, GANs, diffusion and score-based models, flow-based methods, and Schrödinger bridges across representation domains, architectures, conditioning mechanisms, and quality-efficiency trade-offs, complemented by unified controlled experiments.
AI.result: Unified experiments on representative discriminative and generative methods provide controlled empirical evidence characterizing the trade-offs among reconstruction fidelity, perceptual quality, robustness, and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The survey establishes a structured taxonomy and practical roadmap for advancing audio super-resolution from deterministic point estimation to distribution-aware generative modeling, while highlighting emerging directions with LLMs and multimodal foundation models and open challenges in perceptual evaluation, deployment, and real-world generalization.

title: On Measuring Localization of Shortcuts in Deep Networks

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a counterfactual experiment design to measure layer-wise shortcut localization in deep networks and finds that shortcuts are distributed across the network rather than localized to specific layers.
AI.motivation: Shortcuts are spurious rules that perform well during training but fail to generalize, and designing principled mitigation methods requires understanding how shortcuts affect feature representations across layers.
AI.method: The authors introduce shortcut-inducing data skew during training and counterfactually compare models trained on clean versus skewed datasets using shortcut-learning localization metrics across CIFAR-10, Waterbirds, and CelebA with VGG, ResNet, DeiT, and ConvNeXt architectures.
AI.result: Localization metrics show that shortcut learning is distributed throughout the network rather than confined to specific layers, with earlier layers predominantly encoding spurious features and later layers predominantly forgetting core features predictive on clean data; moreover, the localization metrics are associated with the success of layer-wise training interventions.
AI.conclusion: Understanding that earlier layers encode spurious features while later layers forget core features explains layer-wise shortcut behavior and helps guide effective layer-wise training interventions.

title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
summary: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an enumerating posterior-supported prior framework on a three-layer categorical chain to lift out-of-domain errors hidden in null-support sets into a finitely computable first-order error coefficient mu_err.
AI.motivation: Standard measure theory in generative modeling adopts the almost-everywhere convention, which ignores error components carried by null-support sets and can hide out-of-domain errors.
AI.method: The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set using binary-predicate quotient partitions without point elements, a replica-index counting measure to turn surjections into quotient-layer bijections, and an invertible MPT to resolve preimage mutual exclusion, consolidating four results into Theorem 7 via measure descent-recovery.
AI.result: The four results in Theorem 7 establish that binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support, enumerating the morphism itself and accounting for multiplicity as a finitely obtainable first-order error mu_err.
AI.conclusion: The work transforms nontrivial categorical constructions into an engineering-computable, falsifiable first-order error measure for out-of-domain errors previously hidden in null support.

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Dynamical Systems
comment: 19 pages, AIAA SciTech Forum 2027 (Uncertainty Quantification Conference)
summary: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), a non-intrusive reduced-order modeling method that combines limited high-fidelity and abundant low-fidelity snapshots to improve prediction and temporal extrapolation without increasing the training simulation budget.
AI.motivation: Standard Operator Inference (OpInf) requires computationally expensive high-fidelity snapshots, which limits parameter coverage and trajectory duration in aerospace applications and leads to inaccurate or unstable reduced-order models.
AI.method: MF-OpInf uses a control-variates-inspired multifidelity least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across trajectories, while constructing an improved reduced basis from low-fidelity snapshots via weighted proper orthogonal decomposition.
AI.result: Under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to 87% on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem and 28% on 2D incompressible cylinder flow over test regimes extending beyond the high-fidelity training horizon.
AI.conclusion: MF-OpInf improves temporal extrapolation and generalization to unseen parameters for nonlinear dynamical systems without increasing training simulation costs.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for 2D XRD Interpretation Using Simulated and Experimental Data
summary: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with naïve fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a proof-of-concept uncertainty-aware continual learning framework for sequential two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) interpretation using simulated and experimental data.
AI.motivation: Autonomous experimentation systems need characterization models that handle heterogeneous data sources, avoid overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and prevent catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates.
AI.method: The framework combines maximum mean discrepancy domain adaptation for simulation-to-experiment alignment, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN-SNGP) for predictive uncertainty, and replay with knowledge distillation for continual updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on sequential blocks of simulated and experimental XRD patterns for body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed crystal structures, the framework achieves accurate classification, improved domain alignment, reduced forgetting compared with naive fine-tuning, and uncertainty estimates on unfamiliar and noisy inputs.
AI.conclusion: The integrated framework provides a foundation for sequential XRD interpretation in autonomous experimentation, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment left for future work.

title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
summary: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph. We introduce a novel class of clusters called conduits, and present a sound, complete and efficient algorithm for detecting all conduits in the graph. In addition to algorithmic detectability, conduits appear naturally in causal graphs stemming from real-world applications, enabling substantial size reduction. Furthermore, the structure of conduits enables the application of known identifiability results regarding clustering. We demonstrate these properties in a simulation study with real-world graphs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces conduits, a new class of variable clusters in causal graphs, and provides a sound, complete, and efficient algorithm to detect them.
AI.motivation: Clustering variables in causal graphs improves visual clarity and simplifies causal inference, but harnessing this requires an automated method to detect useful clusters.
AI.method: The authors define conduits as a class of clusters whose structure supports existing clustering identifiability results, and design an efficient algorithm to detect all conduits in a graph.
AI.result: In a simulation study using real-world causal graphs, conduits appear naturally, enable substantial graph size reduction, and support known identifiability results.
AI.conclusion: Conduits offer a practical, algorithmically detectable way to simplify real-world causal graphs while preserving identifiability.

title: Training-point consistency of kernel ridge regression with varying correlation scales
summary: The scale parameter in kernel ridge regression plays a pivotal role in modeling the correlation structure of data. In modern applications, sampling density and the underlying correlation range often change simultaneously, making a fixed-scale assumption highly restrictive. However, establishing asymptotic theories under varying scale parameters is fundamentally challenging. To address this gap, this paper develops a unified theoretical framework for kernel ridge regression under varying scale parameters. We establish that, on uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the consistency of the training-point risk holds if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity. This sharp criterion universally covers all regimes along arbitrary deterministic scale sequences, seamlessly unifying the long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range. Furthermore, we provide an explicit, signal-independent construction of a deterministic regularization penalty that guarantees this consistency. Numerical experiments illustrate the criterion and the corresponding penalty across all the three regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a unified theoretical framework for the training-point consistency of kernel ridge regression under varying correlation scale parameters.
AI.motivation: In modern applications, sampling density and correlation range often change together, making fixed-scale asymptotic theories restrictive, while varying-scale asymptotics remain fundamentally challenging.
AI.method: Analyzing uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the authors characterize training-point risk consistency across arbitrary deterministic scale sequences and construct an explicit, signal-independent deterministic regularization penalty.
AI.result: Training-point risk consistency holds if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity, unifying long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range regimes, and numerical experiments illustrate the criterion and penalty across all three regimes.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a sharp, universal criterion and practical regularization construction for kernel ridge regression when correlation scales vary with sampling density.

title: Detection and Classification in Latent Spaces: High-Dimensional Analysis and Validation
summary: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.

AI.tldr: This paper derives high-dimensional large-deviation characterizations for linear and quadratic detectors in foundation model latent spaces, revealing non-monotonic error behavior and enabling prescribed false-alarm control.
AI.motivation: Foundation models yield high-dimensional latent representations where statistical decision rules can be effective, but their behavior in the proportional high-dimensional regime needs analytical characterization.
AI.method: Under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, the authors derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance for linear and quadratic statistics and extend the binary analysis to multi-class classification.
AI.result: Theoretical error probabilities and decay rates exhibit double-descent and multiple-descent phenomena with respect to the shape parameter, and experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models closely match theoretical predictions and accurately predict miss-detection probabilities at prescribed false-alarm levels.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a theoretically grounded, interpretable, and empirically competitive approach to detection and classification in foundation model latent spaces across modalities.

title: LaMe: a Joint Latent Mediation Framework for High-Dimensional Systems
summary: Mediation analysis seeks to understand how an exposure influences an outcome through intermediate variables. However, as increasingly rich datasets become available, hundreds to thousands of potential mediators make these systems difficult to model and hard to interpret. Latent-variable approaches offer a natural way to accommodate these high-dimensional settings. However, existing latent mediation methods face limitations, including overparameterization, biased inference, or limited scalability. We develop LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system through a small number of latent variables. We identify natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the manifest measurements fully capture the latent mediators, and characterize conditions under which the latent representation effectively restricts the observed cross-covariance structure. Simulations assess recovery of observed association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features associated with latent mediation pathways across a range of challenging settings. Four real-world applications demonstrate competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations, including single-dimensional representations of biomarker and proteomic measurements. Together, these results establish LaMe as a practical framework for estimating and summarizing multivariate mediation systems under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian latent mediation framework for estimating and summarizing high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome systems.
AI.motivation: Modern datasets with hundreds to thousands of potential mediators are hard to model and interpret, and existing latent mediation methods suffer from overparameterization, biased inference, or poor scalability.
AI.method: LaMe summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system using a small number of latent variables, identifying natural direct and indirect effects under the assumption that manifest measurements fully capture latent mediators and characterizing conditions on the observed cross-covariance structure.
AI.result: Simulations demonstrate accurate recovery of association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features, while four real-world applications including biomarker and proteomic data show competitive predictive performance with compact, even single-dimensional, latent representations.
AI.conclusion: LaMe provides a practical, scalable framework for multivariate mediation analysis under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.

title: Lipschitz-Constrained Discriminators in Generative Modeling: Asymptotic Behavior and Support Mismatch
summary: We study the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators associated to $L-$Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences of two probability distributions $Q$ and $P$ that interpolate between the rescaled Wasserstein$-1$ metric by some parameter $L>0$ and the KL divergence. The parameter $L$ plays the role of a Lipschitz constraint and is viewed as a regularization parameter: small values of $L$ enforce a more geometry-aware discriminator, while as $L$ increases the geometric regularization is progressively relaxed. It is a known result [3] that such divergences converge to the KL divergence as $L\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the optimal discriminators as $L\to\infty$ in different regimes: Firstly, under $Q\ll P$ and the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ}{dP}$ is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Secondly, when $Q$ and $P$ are discrete distributions satisfying $Q\ll P$, and finally when $Q$ and $P$ are non absolutely continuous discrete distributions. This result motivates training strategies which involve discriminators, such as adversarial generative models. In practice, the data distribution is often represented by a discrete empirical measure, while, especially at the early stages of the training, the model distribution may have little or no overlap with the empirical data distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators for L-Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences as the Lipschitz constraint L approaches infinity across continuous and discrete distribution regimes.
AI.motivation: L-Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences interpolate between rescaled Wasserstein-1 and KL divergence and are used in adversarial generative modeling, where data distributions are discrete empirical measures that may have little or no overlap with model distributions early in training.
AI.method: The authors analyze the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators as L goes to infinity in three regimes: absolutely continuous distributions with bounded Radon-Nikodym derivative, discrete distributions with absolute continuity, and non-absolutely continuous discrete distributions.
AI.result: The analysis establishes the limiting behavior of optimal discriminators under each regime, clarifying how geometric regularization relaxes toward KL divergence under support mismatch.
AI.conclusion: These asymptotic characterizations motivate discriminator-based training strategies in adversarial generative models when model and empirical data supports do not overlap.

title: Mesh-Free Weak-Form Regression for Learning Interaction Kernels from Particle Trajectories
summary: We propose mesh-free weak-form regression for learning interaction kernels from noisy particle trajectories. Our method uses smooth test functions to avoid differentiating noisy data and empirical particle averages to avoid density reconstruction and spatial grids. We then fit sparse combinations of candidate functions, evaluating interaction terms on sampled particle pairs to avoid all-pair quadratic cost. By transferring identifiability from the mean-field limit, we prove high-probability coefficient error bounds that separate finite-particle, time-discretization, observation-noise, and pair-sampling errors, without grid-resolution or density-estimation terms. We evaluate one-dimensional (1D) Newtonian-repulsion, 2D predator-prey, and 10D distance-localized experiments. The numerical results show trends consistent with the theoretical coefficient-error bounds. Comparisons of weak and forward-difference formulations with LASSO, Ridge, and OLS show that weak LASSO gives the smallest coefficient and drift errors in the three nominal experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes mesh-free weak-form regression to learn interaction kernels from noisy particle trajectories with high-probability coefficient error bounds and without spatial grids.
AI.motivation: Learning interaction kernels from noisy particle trajectories typically suffers from noise amplification when differentiating data, costly density reconstruction on spatial grids, or quadratic all-pair evaluation costs.
AI.method: The method uses smooth test functions to avoid differentiation, empirical particle averages to avoid grids and density estimation, and sparse regression over candidate functions evaluated on sampled particle pairs.
AI.result: By transferring mean-field identifiability, the authors prove high-probability coefficient error bounds separating finite-particle, time-discretization, observation-noise, and pair-sampling errors; in 1D Newtonian-repulsion, 2D predator-prey, and 10D distance-localized experiments, weak LASSO achieves the smallest coefficient and drift errors compared with forward-difference formulations and Ridge or OLS.
AI.conclusion: Mesh-free weak-form regression provides a theoretically grounded and accurate approach to learning particle interaction kernels without grid or density-estimation overhead.

title: Node Localization by Multidimensional Scaling with Iterative Majorization
summary: Node localization aims to estimate the positions of nodes based on collected data from other nodes. Depending on the data characteristics, different procedures are utilized to estimate the locations. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive multidimensional scaling algorithm based on iterative majorization that comprises many of the different data characteristics to estimate node locations. The implicitly normalized loss function provides absolute distances and, given anchors, absolute node locations. The algorithm uses a new convergent coordinate descent procedure for the minimization of the majorization function, allowing for a natural treatment of anchors. Optimal transformations of the data seamlessly allows other data than Euclidean distances. Data from multiple sources, resulting in either asymmetric or three-way data, fit the same extensive framework.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a comprehensive multidimensional scaling algorithm based on iterative majorization for node localization across diverse data types and anchor configurations.
AI.motivation: Node localization methods often depend on specific data characteristics, requiring different procedures for Euclidean distances, non-Euclidean transformations, anchors, or multi-source asymmetric and three-way data.
AI.method: The algorithm minimizes an implicitly normalized loss function via a convergent coordinate descent procedure on a majorization function, naturally incorporating anchors, optimal data transformations, and asymmetric or three-way multi-source data.
AI.result: The framework unifies absolute distance and anchor-based location estimation across Euclidean and non-Euclidean data as well as multi-source asymmetric and three-way settings.
AI.conclusion: Iterative majorization with coordinate descent provides a flexible, unified multidimensional scaling framework for node localization.

title: Contrastive latent representation learning with denoising score matching
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Contrastive representation learning methods operate by pulling different views of the same data sample together while pushing them away from views of different samples. A fundamental challenge is the estimation of the repulsive force, which typically requires large batch sizes, can exhibit high variance, and is susceptible to the curse of dimensionality. We introduce ScoreCLR, a contrastive representation learning method that offers a novel way to estimate this repulsion term. We consider the framework of representation learning by maximizing the mutual information between two latent views of a sample. By deriving the gradient of the Shannon entropy with respect to the encoder parameters, we obtain an equivalent objective that involves the score of the latent representation. We then use denoising score matching techniques to estimate this score with a lightweight network that is trained jointly with the encoder. We further propose regularization techniques using different noise levels and a Gaussian prior on the latent representation. ScoreCLR replaces the batch of explicit negative samples in contrastive methods with a learned repulsion whose cost is linear in the batch size rather than quadratic. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 it does so with minimal loss of linear-probe accuracy compared to SimCLR under a shared recipe, while producing projector outputs of higher effective rank, closer to the Gaussian prior.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ScoreCLR, a contrastive representation learning method that replaces explicit negative sample batches with a learned repulsion term estimated via denoising score matching.
AI.motivation: Contrastive learning relies on estimating a repulsive force between samples, which typically requires large batch sizes, suffers from high variance, and scales poorly with dimensionality.
AI.method: Starting from mutual information maximization between two latent views, ScoreCLR derives an equivalent objective involving the score of the latent representation, estimates this score jointly using a lightweight denoising score matching network, and applies multi-noise-level and Gaussian prior regularization.
AI.result: ScoreCLR reduces repulsion cost from quadratic to linear in batch size, and on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 achieves linear-probe accuracy with minimal loss compared to SimCLR while producing projector outputs with higher effective rank closer to a Gaussian prior.
AI.conclusion: ScoreCLR offers a linear-cost alternative to explicit negative sampling in contrastive learning without sacrificing representation quality.

title: Bregman geometry in regular exponential families: dual representations and relative smoothness
summary: Regular exponential-family distributions are ubiquitous in statistics due to their appealing and convenient properties. Notably, they can be expressed in terms of Bregman divergences, revealing fundamental connections between statistics, convex analysis, and information geometry. However, this geometric structure has not been systematically exploited to characterize these distributions with respect to their expectation parametrization. Building on a projective characterization, we establish a general construction of equivalent dual Bregman representations, together with normalization and uniqueness results. These representations express log-densities as ordinary Bregman divergences in dual coordinate systems, providing geometric characterizations of the parameter space. So-called $\beta$- and $\alpha$-scaled dual representations emerge as particular instances of this framework. We further derive dual Bregman representations of conjugate priors and establish that they preserve conjugacy. Applications to classical distributions illustrate the geometric structures underlying seemingly different statistical models. Moreover, we show that these representations provide natural reference geometries for establishing relative smoothness of the primal Bregman representation of the distribution, with explicit bounds that are sharp in the scalar and separable settings. An illustrative application to the Poisson distribution sheds new light on several works in the literature, providing complementary geometric justifications for reference geometries while deriving existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper develops dual Bregman representations for regular exponential-family distributions in expectation parametrization and uses them to establish relative smoothness bounds.
AI.motivation: While regular exponential families are known to connect to Bregman divergences, their geometric structure under expectation parametrization has not been systematically characterized.
AI.method: Building on a projective characterization, the authors construct equivalent dual Bregman representations with normalization and uniqueness results, extend them to conjugate priors while preserving conjugacy, and derive reference geometries for relative smoothness of the primal representation.
AI.result: The framework recovers beta- and alpha-scaled dual representations as special cases, yields sharp relative smoothness bounds in scalar and separable settings, and illuminates existing algorithms and reference geometries in an application to the Poisson distribution.
AI.conclusion: Dual Bregman representations unify statistical, convex-analytic, and information-geometric properties of regular exponential families and provide sharp tools for optimization analysis.

title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
summary: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $\kappa$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $\kappa \rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(\kappa, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces elliptic interpolant schedules and the Zoloflow sampling algorithm for stochastic interpolant generative models, achieving minimax optimal query complexity for Gaussians.
AI.motivation: Generative modeling with stochastic interpolants requires choosing an interpolant schedule and an ODE discretization, but existing choices are not jointly optimized using the analyticity of ODE trajectories.
AI.method: The authors formulate joint schedule and discretization design via conformal mapping of complexified ODE trajectories, yielding variance-preserving elliptic schedules parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions and the Zoloflow sampler based on Zolotarev rational approximants, both incorporating target condition number kappa.
AI.result: For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow is minimax optimal among oblivious score-span algorithms, achieving total-variation error epsilon in Theta(log kappa log(sqrt(d)/epsilon)) score queries; for log-concave targets, it achieves epsilon 2-Wasserstein error in O-tilde(sqrt(d) polylog(kappa, 1/epsilon)) evaluations, and experiments on synthetic and image datasets validate the schedule against alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Conformal-mapping-based elliptic schedules and Zoloflow provide theoretically optimal and empirically effective sampling for stochastic interpolant models.

title: Distributionally Robust Risk Evaluation with Low-Rank Perturbations
summary: We study distributionally robust risk under perturbations restricted to low-rank matrices whose row and column spaces are shared across observations, focusing on how much worst-case risk this restriction sacrifices and how to compute the restricted worst case. Under moment or Wasserstein budgets, we derive quantitative bounds on the gap between the unrestricted and low-rank worst-case risks, characterize when the gap vanishes, and identify the smallest lossless row and column dimensions. To generate worst-case perturbations, we apply projected gradient ascent to a curvature-corrected concave problem and derive computable risk certificates. We establish global sublinear convergence for the corrected objective and linear convergence to a worst-case distribution when the budget constraint is sufficiently active.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes distributionally robust risk evaluation under perturbations restricted to low-rank matrices with shared row and column spaces, bounding the approximation gap and providing convergent algorithms.
AI.motivation: Restricting perturbations to low-rank matrices can make distributionally robust risk evaluation more tractable, but it is unclear how much worst-case risk is sacrificed or how to compute the restricted worst case.
AI.method: Under moment or Wasserstein budgets, the authors bound the gap between unrestricted and low-rank worst-case risks, identify lossless dimensions, and apply projected gradient ascent to a curvature-corrected concave problem to compute perturbations and risk certificates.
AI.result: The analysis characterizes when the low-rank gap vanishes and establishes global sublinear convergence for the corrected objective, plus linear convergence to a worst-case distribution when the budget constraint is sufficiently active.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank perturbation restrictions admit provable risk guarantees and convergent optimization algorithms for distributionally robust risk evaluation.

title: SURFACE: Preference Distribution Matching on Pareto Fronts via Scalarization Steering
summary: Constructing a finite Pareto representation requires allocating a limited number of solutions across the Pareto front (PF). A desired preference distribution specifies this allocation by assigning more solutions to some PF regions and fewer to others. Scalarization generates Pareto solutions by varying objective weights and solving single-objective problems. However, a distribution of scalarization weights generally does not translate into the same distribution of Pareto solutions along the PF, because the weight-to-solution map is nonlinear and unknown in this http URL account for this distortion, we introduce SURFACE (Scalarization Updates for Redistributing Finite Approximations with Chart Estimation}), which adaptively updates scalarization weights to match a desired PF distribution. SURFACE estimates how each region of the weight grid corresponds to an area of the PF from the current scalarized solutions, then redistributes the weights accordingly. The method supports parallel, warm-started, inexact optimization with standard single-objective solvers. Theoretically, we establish that, under the stated regularity conditions, SURFACE achieves linear convergence of the preference distribution mismatch to a finite-resolution error floor of $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/(M-1)})$, where $N$ is the number of adaptive weights and $M$ is the number of objectives. Empirically, experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate improved target-mass balance and PF coverage compared with established baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SURFACE, an adaptive scalarization-weight steering method for matching a desired preference distribution along a Pareto front.
AI.motivation: Uniformly or arbitrarily chosen scalarization weights do not produce the desired distribution of Pareto solutions because the weight-to-solution mapping is nonlinear and unknown.
AI.method: SURFACE estimates the correspondence between weight-grid regions and Pareto front areas from current scalarized solutions and iteratively redistributes weights, supporting parallel, warm-started, inexact single-objective solvers.
AI.result: Theoretically, SURFACE achieves linear convergence of preference distribution mismatch to a finite-resolution error floor of O(N^(-2/(M-1))) for N weights and M objectives; empirically, it improves target-mass balance and Pareto front coverage over baselines across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SURFACE enables accurate, scalable preference-aligned finite approximations of Pareto fronts using standard single-objective solvers.

title: Homogeneous pursuit in $β$ model
summary: Data in forms of networks has been encountered in various prevalent fields at the arrival of big data era. To unveil and recover the true model with core units with numerous links, the $\beta$-model under sparsity constraint is proposed to meet the expectation of statisticians and engineers. Not only does this network model inherit spectacular property from the Erdős-Rényi model, but also exhibits degree heterogeneity through tuning sparsity parameter $s$. In this paper, we propose Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an $\ell_0$-constrained maximum likelihood estimation method implemented through a primal-dual algorithm. To ease the harshness of computation, we find the surrogate function of the corresponding objective function to derive Majorization Minimization algorithm through the primal-dual process. Moreover, after meticulous evaluation, the algorithm brought about captures the property of fine convergence rate in a contraction mapping way. Under some mild conditions, the proposed generalized information criterion (GIC$^*$) for selecting the sparsity level is consistent to find the truth. Combining HP with GIC$^*$ gives the adaptive procedure HP-GIC$^*$; HP-BIC denotes the same estimation method with sparsity selected by BIC. Finally, simulation studies show that GIC$^*$ improves support recovery relative to BIC in the reported comparisons, while HP achieves lower computational cost while maintaining estimation accuracy comparable to the sparse benchmark methods. A microfinance application illustrates the use of HP-GIC$^*$ for studying the association between network prominence and participation, with improved fit in the reported village-level regressions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an l0-constrained maximum likelihood method with a generalized information criterion (GIC*) for sparse degree-heterogeneous beta-model networks.
AI.motivation: Recovering core nodes with many links in large networks requires sparse beta-model estimation, which is computationally challenging under l0 constraints.
AI.method: HP solves l0-constrained maximum likelihood estimation via a primal-dual Majorization-Minimization algorithm using a surrogate objective, paired with a consistent generalized information criterion (GIC*) for sparsity selection (HP-GIC*).
AI.result: The algorithm exhibits contraction-mapping convergence, GIC* is proven consistent for sparsity selection, and simulations show HP-GIC* improves support recovery over BIC (HP-BIC) with lower computational cost than sparse benchmarks; a microfinance application shows improved village-level regression fit.
AI.conclusion: HP-GIC* provides a fast, consistent, and accurate approach for sparse estimation in degree-heterogeneous network models.

title: The Polyak-Łojasiewicz Paper: A 10-Year Retrospective
summary: In 2016, we wrote a paper introducing the phrase "Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition" for an old idea, unsure of how readers would react. The paper ultimately had a larger impact than we expected, and we are surprised and honoured to receive the 2026 PKDD ECML Test of Time Award. With 10 years of hindsight, this note offers an informal and candid retrospective on the PL condition. We take a look back at the origins of the paper, give an AI-assisted refined version of the main theorem, review criticisms of the work, and discuss a variety of related ideas and extensions.

AI.tldr: This note offers a 10-year retrospective on the 2016 paper that named the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition, winner of the 2026 PKDD ECML Test of Time Award.
AI.motivation: The authors reflect on the unexpected impact of naming and popularizing the PL condition a decade after their original 2016 publication.
AI.method: The retrospective reviews the origins of the paper, presents an AI-assisted refined version of the main theorem, addresses criticisms, and surveys related ideas and extensions.
AI.result: The note contextualizes the evolution and reception of the PL condition over ten years of optimization research.
AI.conclusion: The retrospective highlights the lasting influence of the PL condition and its ongoing extensions in optimization.

title: Complex Schrödinger Bridges
summary: Diffusion bridges have emerged as versatile frameworks for facilitating transformations between arbitrary data distributions. However, these approaches are hindered by an immense optimization space and its underlying high-order structures. This paper explores a variant of diffusion bridges for solving real-world problems in complex vector spaces governed by scaling and rotation laws, such as Hamiltonian structures. To address this, we introduce conformal optimal transport (COT), a complex-valued transportation framework designed for physical systems with geometric and dissipative dynamics under a geometric lifting. Building on this, we propose a new class of dynamical diffusion bridges, called complex Schrödinger bridges (CSBs), whose derived algorithms can handle diffusion-based tasks using a conformal geometric prior. For scalability, we propose image-to-image CSB (I$^2$CSB), a tractable diffusion-bridge technique with an analytic spiral posterior. Finally, we implement a physics-informed CSB algorithm within simulations of quantum electrodynamics, mimicking the logical behavior of quantum logic gates. Our extensive results validate the underlying theory while highlighting advantages of complex-valued diffusion.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces conformal optimal transport and complex Schrödinger bridges (CSBs) for diffusion-based transformations in complex vector spaces governed by scaling and rotation laws.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion bridges face immense optimization spaces and high-order structures when applied to physical systems with geometric and dissipative dynamics such as Hamiltonian structures.
AI.method: The authors propose conformal optimal transport (COT) under geometric lifting, derive complex Schrödinger bridges (CSBs) with conformal geometric priors, develop a scalable image-to-image variant (I2CSB) with an analytic spiral posterior, and implement a physics-informed CSB for quantum electrodynamics simulations.
AI.result: Simulations of quantum electrodynamics mimicking quantum logic gates and other experiments validate the theory and demonstrate the advantages of complex-valued diffusion bridges.
AI.conclusion: Complex Schrödinger bridges provide a geometrically grounded and scalable framework for diffusion-based modeling of complex physical systems.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
summary: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural network (PANN) framework to model specimen-to-specimen variability and uncertainty in hyperelastic material laws from scarce, noisy data.
AI.motivation: Hyperelastic laws vary across biological specimens, and pooling data across specimens conflates inter-specimen variability with measurement noise while failing to predict new specimens.
AI.method: Starting from a single-specimen Bayesian PANN, the authors build a hierarchical nonlinear mixed-effects model where specimens share learned polyconvex features and are drawn from a population distribution, inferred jointly via variational inference with a separate noise model.
AI.result: On synthetic populations, the method outperforms three published baselines in population recovery and new-specimen prediction; on Treloar's rubber and healthy/aneurysmal aortas, it matches deterministic PANN accuracy and never misclassifies an aorta cohort with confidence, though it underestimates uncertainty on untested curves.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical Bayesian PANNs separate specimen variability from noise while guaranteeing polyconvexity, enabling uncertainty-quantified predictions for unseen specimens.

title: Small Is Not Dead: Distance-Aware Cluster Revival for e-means
summary: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) is a recent mini-batch k-means algorithm, now part of the FAISS library, that reaches the error of Lloyd's algorithm about an order of magnitude faster on large embedding datasets. Every five mini-batches, it removes every cluster whose running point count falls below a tenth of the average and reuses its centre to split a large cluster. In the authors' ablation, removing this mechanism, called dead-cluster revival, raises the error more than removing any other component added to the moving-average update. The rule, however, considers only cluster size: it cannot distinguish a cluster that is small because it is redundant from one that covers a rare, isolated group of points, and on data with such groups it repeatedly removes centres whose removal is costly. We add a second condition, based on the distance between centres: a small cluster is removed only if its centre is close to another centre, relative to a running estimate of the mean squared error. When a centre equals the mean of its points, this squared distance is an upper bound on the average increase in squared error, per point of the cluster, caused by removing the centre. The condition costs one nearest-centre search for the small clusters every five mini-batches and adds no measurable running time. On the e-means paper's embedding benchmarks, it never prevents a removal, so the results are identical to those of FAISS. On datasets with small isolated groups not used during development, it reduces the test error after two epochs by roughly 10% to 80% relative to count-based revival, and it preserves the advantage of k-means++ initialization; on the other evaluation datasets, it stays within about 1% of the better of revival enabled and disabled. We also report two failure modes that the analysis predicts. This is a CPU proof of concept; GPU implementations are left to future work.

AI.tldr: This paper improves dead-cluster revival in the e-means mini-batch k-means algorithm by adding a distance-aware condition that prevents removing small clusters covering rare, isolated groups.
AI.motivation: e-means removes any cluster whose running point count falls below a tenth of the average, which mistakenly deletes small clusters representing isolated point groups and increases error.
AI.method: The authors add a condition that a small cluster is removed only if its centre is close to another centre relative to a running mean squared error estimate, costing one nearest-centre search for small clusters every five mini-batches.
AI.result: On e-means embedding benchmarks, results are identical to FAISS; on datasets with small isolated groups, the method reduces test error after two epochs by roughly 10% to 80% over count-based revival while preserving k-means++ initialization gains, and stays within about 1% of the better of revival on or off on other datasets.
AI.conclusion: Distance-aware cluster revival protects rare isolated clusters in mini-batch k-means with negligible overhead, with GPU implementation left to future work.

title: DECODE: Decomposable Environments for COntrolled Sequential-Decision Evaluation
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL. Archived release: this https URL
summary: When a sequential decision system falls short of an optimum, its score does not reveal which modifications would improve its decisions. DECODE is a benchmark for testing such modifications through controlled experiments on planning and available information. Its consumer-credit collections generator provides five partially observed environments that share known dynamics matrices and vary a memory parameter and process noise. The experiments change selected inputs or planning rules while keeping the rest of the solver fixed. Each comparison specifies the solver's state inputs, response inputs and planning horizon. On the deterministic base environment, which was selected for a large gap between six-month and one-month planning with the hidden state, extending planning from one to six months increases the scores of two gradient-boosted solvers by 15 to 17 percentage points of the exact optimum, computed with the hidden state and borrower traits. Even at this horizon, the best graded solver, whose repayment response is fitted on logs, remains 15.6 points below that optimum. In a specified intervention sequence, three changes to its state inputs and their evaluation during search lower its score by 6.3 points, and replacing its fitted repayment model with the true response, evaluated with hidden borrower traits, then raises it by 15.6, a net recovery of nine of those points. Because the intermediate effects are conditional on the repayment model and the order of the changes, they do not uniquely assign the gap to separate causes. Within these limits, DECODE makes hypotheses about solver performance testable through specified interventions under known dynamics and explicit information conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DECODE, a benchmark of partially observed consumer-credit collections environments for testing sequential decision-making modifications under controlled dynamics and information conditions.
AI.motivation: When a sequential decision system underperforms, its aggregate score does not reveal which changes to state inputs, response models, or planning horizons would improve decisions.
AI.method: DECODE provides five partially observed environments sharing known dynamics matrices with varying memory and noise, allowing controlled interventions on solver inputs, repayment models, and planning horizons.
AI.result: On the deterministic base environment, extending planning from one to six months raises two gradient-boosted solvers by 15 to 17 percentage points, though the best solver remains 15.6 points below the exact hidden-state optimum; replacing its fitted repayment model with the true response recovers 15.6 points after three state-input interventions had lowered its score by 6.3 points.
AI.conclusion: DECODE enables systematic, controlled hypothesis testing of sequential decision solvers under known dynamics, while noting that intermediate intervention effects depend on ordering and model choice.

title: Dynamic bigraphical Matérn--Whittle processes: learning dependence graphs among spatial-temporal fields
summary: Many studies record several variables at the same sites over a sequence of periods, such as pollutant concentrations at monitoring stations or case counts of infectious diseases by district. A central question concerns the dependence between the variables and its change over time. We develop dynamic bigraphical Matérn--Whittle (DBMW) processes for such data. Each variable has a spatial field that evolves by autoregression. A graph over the variables couples the temporal innovations of the fields. Its links appear and vanish over time, and a link may change sign. A graph Laplacian on the sites gives the spatial structure, and a canonical exponential family links the fields to Gaussian, count or binomial responses. The joint distribution of the latent fields over all sites, variables and periods factorizes over the eigenmodes of the graph Laplacian, and its normalizing constant is free of the graph and of the dynamics. Given the fields, the posterior of the time-varying signed graph is therefore exact, by forward--backward recursions. The estimator has three steps: a fit without a graph, which also gives the switching rates with an interval, the exact graph posterior, and a joint refit. In simulations, DBMW recovers the graph with higher average precision than graphical lasso, time-varying graphical lasso and Poisson log-normal networks, and it predicts withheld data better than a standard spatio-temporal model that fits each variable separately, with a Matérn field and autoregressive evolution, by integrated nested Laplace approximation. In weekly air-quality data from 288 U.S. sites, it recovers the seasonal change of sign between ozone and nitrogen dioxide. In German surveillance data on seven diseases, the district-level links stay positive and stable through the COVID-19 pandemic.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes dynamic bigraphical Matérn-Whittle (DBMW) processes to learn time-varying signed dependence graphs among multiple spatio-temporal fields.
AI.motivation: Studying how dependencies among multiple variables recorded at shared sites evolve over time requires models that handle spatial structure, non-Gaussian responses, and dynamic signed graphs.
AI.method: Each variable's spatial field evolves autoregressively with spatial structure given by a site graph Laplacian, temporal innovations are coupled by a time-varying signed variable graph, and a canonical exponential family links fields to Gaussian, count, or binomial responses; factorization over Laplacian eigenmodes enables exact graph posterior inference via forward-backward recursions in a three-step estimator.
AI.result: In simulations, DBMW achieves higher average precision in graph recovery than graphical lasso, time-varying graphical lasso, and Poisson log-normal networks, and outperforms separate INLA spatio-temporal fits on withheld data; on 288 U.S. air-quality sites it recovers seasonal sign flips between ozone and nitrogen dioxide, and on German disease surveillance data it finds stable positive district links through COVID-19.
AI.conclusion: DBMW provides an exact-posterior, flexible framework for inferring dynamic signed dependence graphs in multivariate spatio-temporal data.

title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
summary: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies numerical rounding and cancellation issues in standard divergences between nearly equal categorical distributions and provides numerically stable reformulations.
AI.motivation: Standard implementations of KL divergence, reverse KL, generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence, Monte Carlo KL, and entropy suffer from rounding and cancellation errors in forward and gradient passes when distributions are nearly equal, affecting distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods.
AI.method: The authors analyze the numerical instabilities in these divergence operations and derive numerically stable reformulations with example implementations.
AI.result: Property-based tests validate the proposed reformulations across forward and gradient computations for nearly equal categorical distributions.
AI.conclusion: The stable reformulations prevent numerical degradation in optimization objectives that rely on divergences between close categorical distributions.

title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
summary: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a mathematical theory of future-task information to explain when finite representations can preserve decision value across infinitely many possible tasks.
AI.motivation: Information systems must often learn representations before knowing future queries, raising the question of when a finite representation suffices for an infinite environment.
AI.method: The authors formalize future-task information via a joint decision-regret state recording posterior action comparisons across permitted tasks, establishing calibrated replacements, information-regret curves, and coding-rate characterizations under compactness assumptions.
AI.result: Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for fixed action counts and singular mass of the source-evidence law for all finite menus; further results show that collective task structure, Fourier-entropy inequalities for parity families, and weighted reach for nested families determine coding rates beyond single-task difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The theory characterizes the shared decision structures that allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many future purposes.

title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
summary: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that hard-filtering stale facts in LLM memory systems can severely hurt downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts, and proposes cost-sensitive deletion.
AI.motivation: LLM memory systems routinely delete facts classified as stale, overlooking the asymmetric risk of mistakenly deleting facts needed to answer queries.
AI.method: The authors run controlled sensitivity and paired targeted interventions across three models, and evaluate a deployment-matched gate on a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split.
AI.result: Hard-drop shifts from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability, with false-drop causing significantly greater degradation than false-keep; on the frozen split, the deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for oracle selection.
AI.conclusion: Memory deletion should be treated as cost-sensitive, validating query-critical false-drop risk on matched data or defaulting to label-free retention when validation is unavailable.

title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
summary: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper audits four hallucination detectors on 4-bit quantized small on-device LLMs, finding that detector rankings invert across models and that TruthfulQA-Generation's standard labeler fails.
AI.motivation: Hallucination detection is mostly evaluated on 7B-70B models with large sampling budgets, leaving practitioners without reliable guidance for 4-bit quantized 2B-3B on-device models.
AI.method: The authors run a reproducible single-T4-GPU audit of token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, semantic entropy, and SelfCheckGPT-NLI on 4-bit NF4 Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct using closed-book TriviaQA and TruthfulQA-Generation.
AI.result: Cross-model detector rankings invert (Spearman rho = -0.80, Kendall tau-b = -0.667), the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from sampling-based consistency detectors under bootstrap 95% CIs, and TruthfulQA-Generation's token-overlap labeler yields near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) despite the same pipeline reaching 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA.
AI.conclusion: Detector rankings from large models do not transfer to small quantized on-device LLMs, and practitioners should treat detector selection as an error-rate allocation problem while avoiding flawed overlap labelers.

title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
summary: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LoRAWeaver, a training-free adapter routing method that selects LoRA adapters by aligning adapter-conditioned query representations with task prototypes in adapter-output space.
AI.motivation: Growing pools of task-specific LoRA adapters complicate inference-time selection, and existing routers often require retraining whenever new adapters are added.
AI.method: LoRAWeaver treats routing as representation alignment in the adapter-output space, matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes via cosine similarity without training a router.
AI.result: On LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B across a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and out-of-distribution tasks, LoRAWeaver outperforms training-free baselines in cross-task routing and approaches a trained retrieval encoder, with ablations confirming the benefit of directional alignment.
AI.conclusion: Directional alignment in adapter-output space enables effective, training-free LoRA routing in dynamic multi-adapter settings.

title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper replaces patient-level nearest-neighbor retrieval in clinical RAG with a tabular population prior from condition-medication co-occurrence statistics for EHR medication set prediction.
AI.motivation: Clinical RAG systems for medication prediction typically retrieve similar patient admissions, which is indirect because the target is a fixed-vocabulary discrete set of medication classes rather than open-ended case reasoning.
AI.method: The authors construct a tabular population prior that ranks medication class candidates using a sparse condition-medication co-occurrence table estimated from training admissions, and swap it into the PACERAG pipeline without changing downstream components.
AI.result: On 1,004 held-out MIMIC-IV admissions, swapping in the tabular prior improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 with no extra LLM calls or inference-time patient index, while a non-LLM top-k baseline reaches F1 = 0.248.
