AI.method: The authors extend DTS—a Monte Carlo tree search over denoising trajectories—to use existing property-conditional models as unbiased guided proposals and to perform multi-objective sampling in a single search.
AI.result: On de novo crystal generation, DTS improves crystal stability, generates structures in rare space groups or with high bulk modulus from pretrained conditional models, and produces Pareto fronts trading off dielectric constant and bandgap without modifying model weights.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time tree search provides a flexible, training-free mechanism for multi-objective steering of scientific diffusion models.

title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
summary: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular ontology and SWRL rule set developed with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living in smart homes.
AI.motivation: Smart homes must coordinate heterogeneous devices to support ageing dwellers, requiring a shared formal representation of both user impairments and smart object capabilities.
AI.method: Derived from two Italian Design For All use cases (cycle-ergometer exercise and accessible kitchen configuration), the authors build a modular ontology using the NeOn methodology, integrating ICF user profiles, fitness metrics, smart object programs, comfort dimensions, and SWRL rules.
AI.result: The resulting ontology and SWRL rules classify user fitness levels, recommend exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and match smart objects to specific user impairments.
AI.conclusion: Use-case-driven ontology engineering with NeOn provides a structured semantic data layer for personalized ambient assisted living systems.

title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
summary: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates ensembling Mixture-of-Experts routers, finding mild validation-loss improvements that are offset by the added computational cost of training multiple routers.
AI.motivation: While neural network ensembles improve accuracy through member diversity, standard Mixture-of-Experts models rely on a single router to weight experts.
AI.method: The authors train ensembles of routers jointly with experts on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks using underparameterized networks, and analyze results via a router performance-diversity decomposition.
AI.result: Adding routers lowers validation loss, explicitly maximizing expert diversity improves mean performance on three of four tasks, maximizing router diversity has no effect, and arithmetic-mean weight combination outperforms geometric mean, though extra router training costs offset the mild gains.
AI.conclusion: Router ensembling offers modest performance benefits that are generally outweighed by its additional training overhead.

title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates image-specific and universal adversarial attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 paired with four object trackers in CARLA, showing severe tracking degradation.
AI.motivation: Adversarial perturbations to object detectors can disrupt downstream Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) trajectory estimation in autonomous vehicles in ways not captured by detection accuracy alone.
AI.method: The authors test image-specific attacks and single Universal Adversarial Perturbations (UAPs) against YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 combined with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT in the CARLA simulator, measuring MOTA, HOTA, and IDF1.
AI.result: Under image-specific attacks, YOLOv3-based trackers drop from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03% HOTA (with MOTA reaching -772.60%), while YOLOv4-based trackers drop to 25.06-26.86% HOTA; image-agnostic UAPs also substantially degrade tracking accuracy across frames.
AI.conclusion: Both frame-specific and universal adversarial attacks pose severe risks to camera-based multi-object tracking in autonomous driving.

title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 First Workshop on Meta Agents: Managing Agents that Manage Agents (Meta-Agents)
summary: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that multi-agent systems like Claude Code and Codex can be broken by forged-record attacks when strong orchestrators delegate to weaker sub-agents.
AI.motivation: AI safety evaluations typically test frontier models in isolation, overlooking vulnerabilities that emerge only when strong orchestrator agents delegate tasks to cheaper sub-agents.
AI.method: The authors plant a forged record in a local file store and test unmodified Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, alongside 18-model aggregator simulations, on question-answering tasks with and without sub-agent delegation.
AI.result: Strong orchestrators searching directly commit nearly zero harmful revisions across 1,000+ trials, but delegating to cheaper sub-agents causes failures in 20/180, 44/180, 75/180, and 553/900 cases; in simulations, five otherwise safe aggregators repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials.
AI.conclusion: The safety of a multi-agent system is governed by its weakest sub-agent rather than its strongest orchestrator.

title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
summary: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers a directional relevance asymmetry in stateless code localization and introduces GraphScent, a training-free search controller that lifts exact localization from 12.8% to 23.4% at 31B.
AI.motivation: Localizing code issues on a single consumer GPU requires short, stateless inspections, but it is unclear which structural code relationships yield informative relevance signals from frozen models.
AI.method: Studying Gemma 4 models on 211 Python issues across 86 repositories, the authors find enclosing scopes and upstream callers separate true neighbors from lexical distractors while downstream callees and peers do not; they build GraphScent to propagate calibrated relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over Typed-AST multigraphs, paired with AST Ripple for co-edit checks.
AI.result: Zero-leakage masked-scope probes confirm the directional asymmetry reflects functional role rather than leakage, and GraphScent's likelihood calibration lifts exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8% to 23.4% at 31B within a single-GPU budget.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting directional structural asymmetry with calibrated likelihood propagation enables effective stateless code localization on local hardware.
